prompt: Which condition characterises bounded shrubdepth using first-order transductions?

answers.text: The class is contained in the outputs of one fixed FO transduction of finite rooted trees whose height has a uniform bound.
answers.explanation: A bounded-height tree-model gives such a transduction using finitely many colours. Conversely, fixed FO interpretations of bounded-height coloured trees have bounded shrubdepth.

answers.text: The class is contained in the outputs of fixed FO transductions of arbitrary finite graphs.
answers.explanation: This is vacuous: the identity transduction already covers every graph class.

answers.text: Every member is a subgraph of some rooted tree of bounded height.
answers.explanation: This excludes dense examples such as cliques. A transduction can create adjacency between leaves.

answers.text: Every member is a minor of some rooted tree of bounded height.
answers.explanation: Minors of trees are forests, so this cannot cover bounded-shrubdepth classes containing triangles.

answers.text: The class is transducible from finite rooted trees of arbitrary height, with no other restriction.
answers.explanation: The identity on all paths already gives an unbounded-shrubdepth output class. A uniform height bound is essential.

answers.text: The class transduces some bounded-height trees.
answers.explanation: This reverses the direction and is too weak: even very complicated classes can output an edgeless graph or one vertex.

answers.text: Each output graph has its own FO transduction from a height-one tree, with no uniform formula bound.
answers.explanation: Any fixed finite graph can be encoded with sufficiently many specially chosen colours. The recipe must be uniform across the class.

answers.text: The class is transducible from trees of bounded degree, allowing unbounded height.
answers.explanation: Paths have bounded degree but unbounded shrubdepth, and the identity transduction preserves them.

answers.text: A fixed FO transduction from bounded-height trees must preserve the original tree edges on its output vertices.
answers.explanation: The interpretation may completely redefine adjacency. Requiring inherited tree edges would rule out dense examples.

answers.text: One fixed finite rooted tree must supply all outputs, although their vertex counts can be unbounded.
answers.explanation: Fixed finite copying and interpretation cannot produce arbitrarily large outputs from one fixed finite input.

sources.title: Ganian et al. — Shrub-depth: Capturing Height of Dense Graphs, §§2–4
Ghasemi et al. — CSL 2026, §2: first-order transductions and monadic dependence
